articles.title: How to Answer a Question You Don't Know on a Sales Call: Sales Tips and Sales Scripts for Founders and Engineers
articles.description: Every founder, solutions engineer and new AE eventually hits the moment: the buyer asks something you can't answer, and your brain goes blank. These sales tips and sales scripts show you how to handle "I don't know" on a sales call without losing credibility, and how to practise it until it feels normal. Done well, a question you can't answer can actually build sales confidence on both sides of the table. Why "I don't know" feels so dangerous If you come from engineering, you're trained to be right. In a code review, guessing is a bad habit. On a sales call, the instinct flips into panic: "If I don't know this, they'll think the product isn't real." So people do one of three things: Bluff. "Yes, we support that." (You're not sure.) This is the one that comes back to hurt you in procurement or onboarding. Ramble. Five minutes of thinking out loud until the original question is lost. Collapse. "Uh, I'm not sure, sorry," followed by a visible drop in energy for the rest of the call. Buyers don't expect you to know everything. They do watch how you behave when you don't. Calm and specific reads as trustworthy. Bluffing reads as risk. The 4-step answer: Acknowledge, Clarify, Commit, Continue Use this simple sales framework whenever you hit a question you can't answer. 1. Acknowledge honestly Say it plainly, once, without apologising three times. "Good question. I don't want to guess on that one." That sentence does more for your credibility than a confident wrong answer. 2. Clarify what they actually need Half the time, the question behind the question is easier than the question itself. Ask one of these discovery questions: "Can I ask what's driving that? Is it something you need on day one, or more of a future concern?" "When you say 'integrates with your CRM,' do you mean syncing contacts, logging calls, or something else?" "Is this a must-have for the decision, or a nice-to-know?" You'll often discover you can answer the real need, or that it's not a blocker at all. 3. Commit to a specific follow-up Vague promises ("I'll look into it") sound like brush-offs. Be specific about who, what and when. "I'll check with our CTO and send you a written answer by Thursday. Who else should be on that email?" Then write it down where they can see you doing it. On video calls, saying "I'm noting that now" is enough. 4. Continue the call Don't let one unknown hijack the conversation. Bridge back to what you were doing: "So I've got that one on my list. Going back to what you said about onboarding new reps, how long does that take today?" Sales scripts for the most common situations The technical deep-dive you can't go into "That's deeper than I can answer accurately right now. I'd rather get you the exact answer than a rough one. Would it help to set up 20 minutes with our engineer next week, or is a written answer enough?" The feature you don't have Don't pretend. Don't over-apologise either. "We don't do that today. Can you walk me through how you'd use it? I want to understand whether it's a blocker or whether there's another way to get you the same result." Pricing or contract terms you're unsure about "I don't want to quote you something I'd have to walk back. Let me confirm the exact terms and send them over tomorrow. In the meantime, is there a budget range you're working within?" Security and compliance questions This is where bluffing is most expensive. "Security questions deserve a precise answer. If you send me your questionnaire, I'll make sure it's filled in properly rather than me paraphrasing on a call." The question that's really an objection in disguise "Do you have customers in our industry?" sometimes means "I'm worried you won't understand us." Answer honestly, then address the worry: "Not yet in your industry specifically. What would you need to see to feel confident we understand how your team sells?" What not to do Don't guess and hope. A wrong "yes" on a call becomes a broken promise in writing. Don't say "great question" to everything. Once is fine. Every time sounds like a stalling tactic. Don't hand over control. "I don't know, what do you think?" without structure makes you sound lost, not curious. Don't forget the follow-up. The answer you promised is now part of your sales pitch. Missing it costs more than not knowing. A quick pre-call checklist Before any important sales call, spend five minutes on this: [ ] List the three questions you'd least like to be asked. [ ] For each one, decide: can I answer it, or do I need a "clarify and commit" script? [ ] Know who on your team can answer technical, pricing and security questions, and how fast. [ ] Have one bridge sentence ready to bring the call back on track. [ ] Decide in advance what you will never promise on a call (custom features, discounts, timelines). How to practise it Reading the 4 steps is easy. Doing them while a buyer is waiting for an answer is not. That moment of blank-mind panic is a reflex, and reflexes change with sales practice, not with notes. A simple drill for founders and teams: Ask a colleague to play the buyer and fire five hard questions at you, at least two of which you genuinely can't answer. Run the 4 steps out loud for each one. No pausing to think about the framework. Record it. Listen for apologies, rambling, and whether you actually got back to the call. Swap roles. Playing the buyer teaches you how calm "I don't know" sounds from the other side. Repeat it a few times and the first sentence ("I don't want to guess on that one") becomes automatic. That's the point: when the panic arrives, your mouth already knows what to do. Key takeaways Buyers judge how you handle not knowing more than the gap itself. Acknowledge, clarify, commit, continue. Use discovery questions to find the real need behind a hard question. Never bluff on features, pricing or security. Rehearse with sales role play until the response is a habit. If you want a place to practise hard questions like these against virtual customers who push back, that's what we're building at Kulissa.

articles.title: 40-image mood boards get 'let us think.' 3+3+1 sentence locks form direction
articles.description: Most mood boards fail on quantity. Forty pictures pasted into a collage show the client forty possible directions, and the only honest answer to that is "nice, let's look some more". A board that actually settles the direction has three parts on one page, and if any one of them is missing the page turns into wallpaper. The first part is three anchor images, each paired with a word. Three is a constraint that forces a decision: if the three do not point the same way, the direction is not thought through yet, and the board is simply hiding that. The word matters more than the image, because words are what people remember and repeat. It also has to be specific enough to be rejected. "Premium" is not a word in this sense - nobody can argue against it, so it excludes nothing. "Like a laboratory instrument" is a word: it rules out rounded consumer-electronics language, it can be checked against a sketch, and two people will disagree about it, which is exactly when a direction gets clarified. The second part is three counter-examples. Positive references say "go this way"; negative references say "do not go that way", and the negative ones carry more weight in a review, because they eliminate wrong answers directly. When somebody looks at a proposal and says it resembles one of the counter-examples, the judgement takes one sentence. Choose them carefully: do not pick ugly products, pick the ones that look good but are not what you want, because those are the only ones with discriminating power. Three successful competitors are usually the best pick, since the client has probably praised them somewhere else and needs the record cleared. The third part is the sentence, and it is the real deliverable. The client goes back and briefs their own boss; they will not remember your pictures, but they can remember twenty characters. "Like an instrument, not an appliance" can be compared against a drawing and drawn out. "Precise, restrained, professional" cannot - it is a pile of adjectives, and every listener reconstructs a different product from it. Read the sentence aloud once; if it does not roll, it will not survive the second hand-off, and the direction drifts at exactly that point. Two practical limits. Put 2 or 3 real material samples or close-up shots on the page so that "how it feels in the hand" is not argued in the abstract, but keep the whole page at 8 to 10 items; more than that and the attention scatters. If your content does not fit, you are trying to set more than one direction, and it should be two sessions. One page, one direction.

articles.title: Your AI Tools Are Getting Smarter. Why Does Your Work Still Feel So Fragmented?
articles.description: Switching models is easy. Keeping your decisions, project context, and next steps connected is the harder problem. You ask one AI to research an idea, another to challenge it, and a third to help you write. Then you become the courier. You copy the brief. Explain the decisions. Remind each tool what you already ruled out. Somewhere along the way, you lose the version you liked and start searching through old conversations. The answers might be useful. The process still needs work. I know this frustration because it’s part of why we started building 9xchat at the end of 2024. Disclosure: I’m a co-founder of 123sudo, the team behind 9xchat. This is both a workflow problem I care about and a product I help build. Back then, I could feel my work becoming tied to one AI app. My chats were there. My project context was there. The background I had spent time explaining was there. Trying another model was possible. Taking that accumulated understanding with me was harder. That made me question what I actually needed from AI. Was it another place to ask questions, or a better system for continuing the work? The work between the answers A quick question doesn’t need much continuity. A project does. When you’re building something over days or weeks, each conversation sits inside a larger story. There’s an audience you chose, an approach you rejected, a deadline you’re working toward, and a reason the latest draft looks the way it does. An individual answer can be excellent and still miss that story. You ask for a launch plan, and it recommends a channel you’ve already ruled out. You ask for a revision, and it changes something you deliberately kept. You start a new conversation and spend the opening messages rebuilding the brief. None of these moments looks dramatic on its own. Together, they make working with AI feel strangely repetitive. You’re not just doing the project. You’re maintaining the explanation of the project. That is the work between the answers. A better model is not automatically a better workflow Model capability matters. Different tasks benefit from different strengths, and choosing the right model can make a real difference. But model quality and workflow quality are not the same thing. A more capable model still needs relevant information. If it doesn’t have your current constraints or the reasons behind your decisions, you may get a polished answer that takes the project in the wrong direction. The question isn’t only: Which model should I use? It’s also: What does this model need to know so we can continue instead of starting again? That second question gets less attention, but it has become central to how I work. I don’t want every conversation to begin with a longer prompt. I want a reliable way to carry forward what matters, inspect it, and change it when the project changes. Before adding another tool, trace one task If your AI setup feels fragmented, start by looking at one real task. Choose something you recently completed: a proposal, an article, a research brief, a feature plan. Follow it from the first question to the finished result. Where did you repeat yourself? Look for the background information you explained more than once. Was it the audience? The tone? A technical constraint? A decision you thought was already settled? Repeated explanations show you which context needs a more deliberate home. What did you move between tools? Not every copy and paste is a problem. Sometimes a specialist tool is worth the handoff. But notice when you’re moving information simply because the next tool has no other way to access it. That’s coordination work. It deserves to be counted as part of the cost of your setup. Which decisions disappeared? Finding an old answer isn’t always enough. You also need to know whether it still applies. What did you choose? Why? What changed afterward? A saved transcript contains the conversation. It doesn’t necessarily give you a clear record of the current decision. What did each tool contribute? Some tools earn their place through a capability you genuinely need. Others remain in your workflow because you’ve become used to working around them. The point isn’t to force everything into one app. It’s to make sure the handoffs are helping you, rather than quietly becoming another job. ** Keep the useful context, not everything** My goal isn’t to make an AI remember every sentence I’ve ever written. It’s to make the right information available when it matters. For an ongoing project, I’d start with four things. The brief: What are we making, who is it for, and what should it accomplish? The constraints: What limits the work? Budget, tone, technical requirements, deadlines, or approaches we’ve ruled out. The decisions: What have we chosen, and why? The next action: Where did we stop, and what needs to happen next? Here’s a simple example: Project: An article for independent builders using multiple AI tools. Goal: Help readers identify where their workflow loses context. -Constraints: Practical rather than speculative. No invented productivity claims. Decision: Lead with the reader’s frustration, not the product’s features. Next action: Review the draft for unsupported claims and unnecessary promotion. That’s a small amount of information, but it gives the next conversation somewhere useful to begin. You can keep a project record like this in a document or a note. You don’t have to change tools to start working more deliberately. The system matters before the software does. Why we started building 9xchat At the end of 2024, the problem felt clear to me: I was investing time in conversations, but too much of their value felt tied to the app where they happened. I didn’t want choosing a different model to mean rebuilding my working context. That frustration helped push us to build 9xchat. Since then, it has evolved into an agentic workspace with multiple models, memory, notes, tools, Skills, and MCP connections. But the most meaningful change for me isn’t the growing feature list. It’s how much I now build with it. I use 9xchat every day, and I find it hard to imagine my working routine without it. Not because it does everything for me, but because it has become part of how I develop ideas and move work forward. That experience has made something very clear to me: The model matters. The system you build around it matters, too. What the system adds** In 9xchat, I can switch models within a conversation rather than treating each model as a completely separate working environment. Memory gives relevant information a way to persist beyond a single exchange. Notes provide a place for material I want to keep deliberately. Agents and reusable prompts help define recurring ways of working. These are different jobs. A note isn’t the same as a memory, and neither replaces checking the current brief. The distinction becomes even more important as the workspace gains more capabilities. The public documentation separates three building blocks: Tools let the assistant perform specific actions, such as searching the web or working with notes. Skills provide instructions for how it should approach a task or structure an answer. MCP connections make external tool collections available to the assistant. Tools, Skills, and MCP use in chat are part of Pro. To me, their value isn’t simply that the AI can do more things. It’s that they can support a more coherent way of working: relevant context, an appropriate method, and access to the tools needed for the task. That still requires judgment. A connected tool isn’t automatically the right tool. Saved information isn’t automatically current. A successful action isn’t proof that the entire task is correct. Being able to inspect and question the work remains essential. Using it is part of building it** At 123sudo, there’s always something to build or improve. Using 9xchat daily keeps showing me where the next improvement should be. Where did I have to repeat myself? What took too many steps? What did I expect the workspace to understand that it didn’t? Those moments are useful feedback precisely because they interrupt real work. I’m not only looking at the product from the outside. I’m inside it, trying to get something done, noticing what helps and what gets in the way. That doesn’t make my experience representative of everyone’s. We now have more than 1,000 users, bringing different projects, habits, and expectations. Their feedback matters alongside our own. People are also paying for access through monthly and lifetime licenses. That adds responsibility. A workspace has to earn its place through use, not just through a convincing demo. For clarity, Pro access and AI usage are separate: the current pricing offers monthly, yearly, and lifetime Pro options, while 9xchat AI credits are purchased separately. The ambition is bigger than the current product** One day, I’d love for 9xchat to help manage and coordinate far more of the systems we use at 123sudo. But that is a direction we want to explore, not a claim that it can run everything today. Broader capabilities need careful development: clear permissions, dependable behavior, ways to verify actions, and boundaries around what should require a person’s approval. Skills and MCP support are already here. What we build on top of them still needs to evolve through testing, feedback, and real use. I’m excited about that future. I’m also interested in the smaller improvements that make tomorrow’s work less frustrating than today’s. Sometimes that means another capability. Sometimes it means making an existing workflow clearer, more reliable, or easier to control. The milestone I’m proudest of** 9xchat is the first digital app I’ve helped build that I use every single day. Not just to test it. To do my own work. There’s something meaningful about helping build a tool and then repeatedly choosing it when you have something real to finish. I still see the rough edges. I still have ideas for what it should do better. In a way, that’s the point: using it keeps me close to the problem we started with. I wanted my work with AI to feel less scattered. I wanted to spend less effort carrying context and more effort building on it. That remains the goal. The next leap might be a more connected way of working A more capable model can open up new possibilities. I’m not dismissing that. But I no longer expect a model upgrade alone to fix a fragmented working process. If your brief is scattered, your decisions are buried, and every new conversation requires another introduction, the system around the model deserves attention too. Start with one project. Keep its brief current. Record the decisions that matter. Make the next action clear. Then judge your setup by a practical question: When you return to the work, can you continue, or do you have to explain it all again? Try keeping one project’s context connected in 9xchat.

articles.title: Our Network Supplier's Mistake Stopped Every Branch for a Day and Its Contract Capped What It Owed Us at Three Months of Fees
articles.description: A managed service provider runs our branch network, including the routers and firewalls at all thirty eight branches. In February 2025 one of its engineers applied a firewall change at six in the morning that blocked every branch from reaching our trading system. It was found and reversed shortly after two in the afternoon. For eight hours our counters took orders on paper, and some customers went elsewhere. Finance estimated the lost margin, overtime and credit notes at a little over two hundred thousand pounds. At the next board meeting our chief executive asked how much of that we would recover. I had to find out, and the answer was in a clause I had never read properly. The provider's total liability for any claim in a year was capped at the charges we had paid it in the previous three months, about thirty six thousand pounds. Loss of profit, revenue and business were excluded altogether, and those made up almost all of our loss. For failures to meet the service levels, the service credits were stated to be our sole remedy, and that day earned us about four thousand pounds. Our lawyers advised that a claim for negligence would meet the same cap. I had negotiated that contract in 2021 with our procurement team. I read the service level schedule line by line and left the liability clause to our lawyers, who reviewed it as a standard term, which it was. Nobody had asked them to compare it with what an outage would cost us, because nobody had worked that out. The board had assumed that outsourcing the network had moved the risk of it failing to someone else. Most of it had stayed with us. Every contract for a service whose failure can stop us trading now comes to the board with a one page summary prepared with finance. It states what a day without the service would cost us, what the supplier would pay in that case, and the gap we would carry. That gap is then either covered, negotiated down or accepted by name. At its renewal this year, our network contract's cap rose to twelve months of fees, and changes to branch firewalls now need our approval before they are applied. Outsourcing a service does not outsource the loss when it fails. The liability clause tells you how much of that loss you are still carrying, so read it with your finance director as well as your lawyer. – Serguey Shinder

articles.title: Music Customer Tag Management System Architecture & Design
articles.description: Music Customer Tag Management System Architecture & Design ——For Music Streaming Applications (Deliverable Solution) Background & Business Pain Points Music streaming apps accumulate massive user behavior data: song playback, search, collection, playlist creation, sharing, subscription payment, in-app interaction, etc. Most platforms face the following common problems: 1. Identity fragmentation: Users log in across mobile APP, in-car audio, smart speakers, WeChat mini-programs; anonymous users convert to registered users, leading to scattered user profiles. 2. Unstandardized tags: Different teams (recommendation, operation, membership) define tags independently, causing inconsistent metrics (e.g., "active user" has multiple definitions). 3. Imbalance between real-time & offline computing: Pure offline tags cannot support real-time recommendation & instant marketing; pure real-time tags lack global accuracy for large-scale crowd segmentation. 4. Weak tag governance: No version management, data lineage tracing, lifecycle expiration or access permission control, leading to redundant tags and data compliance risks. 5. Difficult business integration: Tags cannot be directly invoked by recommendation engines, push systems, marketing tools, resulting in low business value conversion. This solution designs a closed-loop tag management system to solve the above pain points. Core Architecture Philosophy 2.1 Unified Music Identity (MID) Construct a globally unique Music ID (MID) as the master user identifier. Map device ID, mobile number, third-party OAuth ID (WeChat/Apple/Google), anonymous session ID to one MID. Support anonymous user → registered user identity merging Link user behavior across all terminals (mobile, car, smart device, PC) MID serves as the only association key for all tag data 2.2 Full-Cycle Tag Metadata Governance Every tag must be pre-defined with complete metadata before going online: Metadata Item Description Example Tag ID & Name Unique identifier & readable name tag_001_music_taste_pop Business Purpose Which business scenario it serves Personalized recommendation / Membership churn intervention Tag Category Factual / Statistical / Rule-based / Model Statistical tag Calculation Logic SQL / Flink rule / ML model inference logic Count play times of pop songs in last 30 days Update Mode Offline full / Real-time incremental / Hybrid Hybrid Update Frequency Daily / Hourly / Second-level Daily offline + real-time incremental Data Owner Team responsible for the tag Recommendation Algorithm Team Effective & Expiration Time Tag lifecycle Valid from 2026-11-01 to 2027-11-01 Retention Period How long historical snapshots are kept 180 days Data Lineage Source tables & upstream dependencies User play log table ods_user_play_log Permission Level Public / Internal / Sensitive (PII) Sensitive (requires approval) 2.3 Hybrid Computing Model: Offline Full Recomputation + Real-time Incremental Update Offline pipeline: Generates stable baseline tags via batch computing. It is the source of truth for tag data. Used for large-scale audience segmentation, tag quality verification, historical trend analysis, and ML model training. Real-time pipeline: Processes user behavior events with low latency, updates lightweight tags incrementally, and overwrites the offline baseline for online query. Reconciliation mechanism: Periodically compare offline baseline and real-time incremental tag values, repair inconsistent data automatically. Tag versioning: Each tag calculation generates a version number; downstream services can specify a tag version to ensure result reproducibility. 2.4 Four-Dimensional Tag Classification (Mapped to Music Business) Tag Type Definition Music App Typical Examples Computing Mode Factual Tags Objective attributes directly collected from source data, no complex calculation Gender, age, city, registration channel, device model, membership level (free/paid/VIP), subscription expiry date, registration time Real-time / Near real-time Statistical Tags Aggregated metrics derived from user behavior over a sliding time window 30-day play count, average daily listening duration, top 3 favorite genres, favorite artists, playlist creation times, search frequency, weekly new song playback ratio Offline daily + real-time incremental Rule-based Tags Tags defined by explicit business rules combining multiple conditions High-value potential user (VIP expired within 30 days + 30-day play >100 times + no re-purchase), Churn-risk user (no login in 7 days + listening duration dropped by 50%), Night owl listener (play peak 23:00–02:00), Indie music enthusiast Offline full / Real-time rule engine Model Tags Tags generated by machine learning models Music taste embedding vector, churn probability score, price sensitivity level, genre preference score, ad tolerance level, potential paid conversion probability Offline batch inference / Online model serving Layered System Architecture The system adopts a five-layer architecture, from bottom to top: Layer 1: Data Source Layer Collect raw data from all touchpoints of the music app: User behavior logs: Play, pause, skip, search, collect, download, share, comment, playlist create/delete, radio tune-in User profile data: Registration info, bound phone, profile settings, minor mode status Transaction data: Subscription order, in-app purchase, coupon usage, refund records Content metadata: Song, artist, album, genre, language, release year, tag of songs Context data: Login time, geo location (optional, privacy-compliant), device type, network type, in-car / smart speaker terminal mark Data is collected via SDK, server logs, and binlog, then sent to Kafka as the unified data bus. Layer 2: Data Integration & Identity Resolution Layer Data Cleaning: Deduplication, invalid data filtering, format normalization MID Mapping Service: Map device ID / anonymous ID / third-party ID to unified MID; handle ID merging when anonymous users register Data Standardization: Unify behavior event formats, align dimension data (song ID → genre / artist) Layer 3: Tag Computing Layer Offline Computing Engine: Spark / Hive, executes full tag recalculation on a daily/weekly schedule Real-time Computing Engine: Flink, consumes Kafka behavior events, updates tags in near real-time Rule Engine: Executes rule-based tag logic, supports dynamic rule configuration without code release ML Model Service: Loads trained music taste / churn prediction models, executes batch & online inference Tag Version Controller: Manages tag version generation, snapshot creation, version rollback Data Quality Checker: Verifies tag coverage, null rate, outlier detection before tag release Layer 4: Tag Storage & Index Layer Storage Component Stored Content Purpose HBase / ClickHouse Detailed tag values for each MID (latest version + historical versions) Online point query & batch query Elasticsearch Inverted index of tag values Fast audience segmentation (filter users by tag conditions) MySQL / PostgreSQL Tag metadata, tag version info, data lineage, permission config Management console query HDFS Tag snapshots, historical backup, audit logs Disaster recovery & compliance audit Redis Hot user tag cache Low-latency real-time query (P99 < 20ms) Layer 5: Service & Application Layer Tag Query API: get_user_tags (single user), batch_get_user_tags (batch users), get_tag_metadata Audience Segmentation Engine: Visual rule builder, supports AND/OR/NOT conditions, segment estimation, segment export, scheduled refresh Tag Management Console: Web UI for tag creation, editing, version management, lifecycle configuration, data quality monitoring, usage statistics Permission & Audit Service: RBAC access control, sensitive tag approval flow, full operation audit log Data Export Service: Export audience ID lists to recommendation engine, push notification system, CRM, marketing platform End-to-End Data Pipeline Design 4.1 Offline Full Recomputation Pipeline (Daily Baseline) 1. Extract raw data from data warehouse (user logs, order data, content metadata) 2. Execute MID identity resolution to unify user IDs 3. Run Spark jobs to calculate statistical / rule-based / model tags 4. Data quality check: coverage rate > 95%, null value rate < 1%, outlier filtering 5. Write tag results to HBase & Elasticsearch, generate daily snapshot to HDFS 6. Tag version is marked as baseline, open to downstream services 4.2 Real-time Incremental Update Pipeline (Low Latency) 1. User behavior events (play, collect, subscribe) are sent to Kafka in real time 2. Flink job consumes events, updates incremental tag values (e.g., real-time play count, latest favorite genre) 3. Write updated tags to Redis (hot cache) and HBase 4. Overlay incremental results on the offline baseline for online query 5. Send change events to notify downstream recommendation & push systems 4.3 Hybrid Synchronization & Reconciliation Every 1 hour, run reconciliation tasks to compare offline baseline tags and real-time The return URL is not a payment confirmation
articles.description: A checkout we reviewed marked orders as paid when the customer landed on /return?status=success after 3DS. It looked fine in testing, because the redirect and the gateway result always agreed. In production they drifted apart in three ways: The customer pressed Back during the challenge and later reopened the return URL from browser history. The order flipped to paid on a stale redirect. The bank's ACS confirmed the challenge, but the authorization then declined at the issuer. The redirect still said the 3DS step succeeded, so the order was marked paid while no money moved. Anyone could edit the query string. Changing status=failed to status=success worked on a test order, because the handler never checked a signature. The redirect only tells you the browser came back. It says nothing about the transaction. What we changed: the return page now shows "checking your payment" and never writes order state. State changes only from the signed webhook, or from a server-side status call by transaction id when the webhook is late. The page polls our own order status for up to about 20 seconds, then tells the customer we'll email them. The unpaid-but-shipped orders stopped, and so did the paid-but-not-fulfilled ones. Do you let the return URL touch order state at all, or is that strictly webhook territory in your system? Payneteasy handles this kind of payment flow for merchants and PSPs — see how it works.

articles.title: Pull the top pumpfun traders and what they are buying from a free public API, in TypeScript
articles.description: Most pumpfun APIs return new coins. A different question is more interesting to a developer: which accounts made the most realized profit over the last 30 days, and which coins are several tracked traders buying right now? This post answers both with two plain GET requests and about 100 lines of TypeScript. No key, no scraper, no library. The output is two small tables, and a saved fixture lets you reproduce the numbers printed below. Disclosure: I am the founder of copy.top. The API used here is copy.top's own free public API. copy.top is independent and not affiliated with pump.fun or fomo. Setup The files are TypeScript and run on Node 22.6 or newer with type stripping (tested here on Node 24.7): node --experimental-strip-types run.ts Imports between files need the .ts extension, and types use import type, which this mode requires. For plain JavaScript, rename to .mjs, delete the annotations and the import type lines. The two endpoints The REST API is documented on the developers page and, for pumpfun specifically, on the pumpfun API page. Everything is a GET that returns JSON, with no key. The public limit is about 20 calls a minute and answers are cached for up to a minute, so there is no point in polling faster than that. GET https://copy.top/v1/traders?platform=pumpfun&window=30d&sort=realized&limit=10 returns a leaderboard. window is the period, sort=realized ranks by realized profit, limit is the number of rows. GET https://copy.top/v1/coins/hot?window=1h returns coins that tracked traders bought in the last hour, with counts and dollar totals. I checked the field names below against real responses. A trader row has handle, name, pnl, realized, unrealized, roi, winRate (a number from 0 to 1), closed (closed positions), followers, copiers and a few more. A coin row has symbol, token (the address), traders, topTraders, topStillIn, sold, boughtUsd, soldUsd, firstBuyMinAgo, lastBuyMinAgo and buyers. A handle that starts with pf_ is a pumpfun account. Types Only the fields the script reads. export interface Trader { handle: string; name: string; pnl: number; realized: number; unrealized: number; roi: number; winRate: number; // 0 to 1 closed: number; // closed positions in the window followers: number; copiers: number; url: string; } export interface Leaderboard { window: string; sort: string; traders: Trader[]; export interface HotCoin { chain: string; token: string; // address symbol: string; mcap: number | null; traders: number; // tracked traders who bought it in the window topTraders: number; // how many of them are top traders topStillIn: number; // top traders still holding sold: number; boughtUsd: number; soldUsd: number; firstBuyMinAgo: number; lastBuyMinAgo: number; buyers: string[]; export interface HotCoins { at: string; coins: HotCoin[]; Step 1: a small fetch wrapper The wrapper does three things: it builds the query string, it stops a hung request after 20 seconds with AbortSignal.timeout, and it throws on a non-200 answer. The second function waits 1.5 seconds before it calls, which keeps a run far below the public limit. import type { Leaderboard, HotCoins } from "./types.ts"; // polite: the public limit is about 20 calls a minute async function get<T>(path: string, params: Record<string, string | number>): Promise<T> { return (await res.json()) as T; export async function getLeaderboard(limit = 10): Promise<Leaderboard> { return get<Leaderboard>("/traders", { platform: "pumpfun", window: "30d", sort: "realized", limit, }); export async function getHotCoins(): Promise<HotCoins> { await sleep(DELAY_MS); return get<HotCoins>("/coins/hot", { window: "1h" }); A run makes exactly two requests. Step 2: the runner With no argument the script calls the live API. With --fixture it reads fixture.json instead and makes no network call. With --save it also writes the live answers to fixture.json. The second table filters the coins with traders >= 3, so only coins where several tracked traders bought in the last hour remain. Some coins have a blank or invisible symbol, so label falls back to the first characters of the address. import { readFileSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs"; import { getLeaderboard, getHotCoins } from "./api.ts"; let board: Leaderboard; let hot: HotCoins; else { board = await getLeaderboard(10); hot = await getHotCoins(); /[A-Za-z0-9]/.test(c.symbol) ? c.symbol : c.token.slice(0, 6); Live use is node --experimental-strip-types run.ts. Reproduce the numbers Live data changes every minute, so the output of a live run will not match this article for long. I ran the script once against the live API with --save, which wrote fixture.json, and then printed the output below from that fixture: node --experimental-strip-types run.ts --fixture If you copy fixture.json next to run.ts (it is the raw JSON of that one live run, 2026-11-19), you get the same two tables, line for line. name │ realized_usd │ win_rate │ closed │ ├─────────┼──────┼───────────────────┼───────────────────┼──────────────┼──────────┼────────┤ │ 0 │ 1 │ 'pf_c311d04abf73' │ 'supermandev' │ '794,629' │ '97%' 'pf_5482d0f6ab22' │ 'MemeHubCo' │ '114,098' │ '32%' │ 41 │ └─────────┴──────┴───────────────────┴───────────────────┴──────────────┴──────────┴────────┘ coins bought by 3 or more tracked traders, last 1h (as of 2026-11-19T09:55:16.608Z) ┌─────────┬──────────────┬─────────┬─────┬──────────────┬────────────┬───────────┬──────────────────┐ │ (index) │ coin │ traders │ top │ top_still_in │ bought_usd │ sold_usd │ last_buy_min_ago │ ├─────────┼──────────────┼─────────┼─────┼──────────────┼────────────┼───────────┼──────────────────┤ │ 0 │ 'DCTY' │ 55 │ 15 │ 11 │ '265,881' │ '112,627' │ 1 │ │ 1 │ 'APOCRYCOIN' │ 27 │ 6 │ 4 │ '11,814' │ '9,306' │ 2 │ │ 2 │ 'DacityCoin' │ 19 │ 7 │ 4 │ '19,820' │ '5,118' │ 4 │ │ 3 │ '7Aasrt' │ 9 │ 4 │ 3 │ '2,472' │ '991' │ 1 │ │ 4 │ '3B8dDC' │ 33 │ 12 │ 3 │ '22,079' │ '13,040' │ 3 │ │ 5 │ 'GRS' │ 10 │ 6 │ 3 │ '2,533' │ '1,312' │ 8 │ │ 6 │ '48r1TbEV' │ 8 │ 3 │ 2 │ '1,545' │ '1,435' │ 2 │ │ 7 │ 'Sparrow' │ 15 │ 3 │ 2 │ '3,450' │ '1,760' │ 1 │ └─────────┴──────────────┴─────────┴─────┴──────────────┴────────────┴───────────┴──────────────────┘ Reading the tables In the first table, check one thing by hand: realized_usd is the profit from positions closed in the 30 day window, so it is a sum of finished trades, not a value of what the account holds. The raw pnl field also includes open positions, which are marked at the current price. That is why the sort is on realized and not on pnl. Look at the win_rate and closed columns together. Row 1 has a 97% win rate over 34 closed positions, and row 4 has 97% over 1022. Those are very different amounts of evidence, and a win rate says nothing about how large the losses are compared with the wins. Rows 5, 6, 7, 9 and 10 show win rates between 32% and 56%, next to large realized totals: a low win rate can still make money if the wins are big. In the second table, traders is how many tracked traders bought the coin in the last hour, top is how many of those are top traders, and top_still_in is how many of them still hold. Compare bought_usd with sold_usd: for every coin on the list, both are well above zero, so people are already selling while others buy. The last column says how recent the latest buy is. These are counts of past activity at one moment, not a list of things to buy. Where to take it next Add GET /v1/traders/{handle} to read one trader in detail, or poll GET /v1/alerts with the cursor it returns. Writing the results to a file once a day lets you compare rankings from one week to the next. The same data is exposed as an MCP server at https://copy.top/mcp, if you would rather query it from an AI agent than from code. What this does not tell you Realized profit is a window, not a record. A 30 day number is a snapshot of one month. The person at the top this month can be absent next month. A win rate is not an edge. A high rate can come from many tiny wins and a few big losses. Always read it next to the number of closed positions. Buying is not endorsing. A tracked trader buying a coin tells you that one account bought it, at a price you do not get, at a time that has passed. Others in the same hour were already selling. Cached and delayed. Answers can be up to a minute old, and the trades behind them are older still. Past performance does not predict results. Nothing here is financial advice, and copying a trader can lose money, including everything you put in. diogenicious

articles.title: How AIClaw 3.12.14 Shows Sub-Agent Progress Without Leaving the Parent Chat
articles.description: A parent agent can delegate a review and keep working while the child runs. From the parent chat, it is useful to see whether the review is still running and what the child has recorded, especially when several tasks are underway. AIClaw v3.12.14 adds a read-only sub-agent view to the desktop conversation details panel. Release notes Follow the task tree from the parent chat On a desktop viewport at least 1,280 CSS pixels wide, open Conversation Details in an existing chat. If that chat has delegated sessions, the panel lists them by task title and status. A child that delegates work of its own appears with another level of indentation. The renderer builds this tree from session parent IDs. Two sessions in the same workspace can have different task trees. Desktop layout · Sub-agent panel Selecting a child opens its transcript inside the panel. The renderer requests that child's saved history and combines it with live timeline entries by entry ID, giving the live copy precedence when an ID appears in both. A live turn can show a running or interrupted state while the parent chat stays open. When there is no live status, the panel can use the status supplied with the session summary. Panel implementation · Session summaries What the panel and tests cover The panel reads history and renders text and expandable steps. Opening it leaves the active conversation in place and does not resume the child. The Electron smoke fixture checks stored history, verifies that no child resume call occurs, and injects turn events to check running and interrupted states. A Go collaboration test separately checks that a completed child can be identified after returning an answer. These checks use fixtures. They cover the read-only interaction and status transitions, while the quality and timing of delegated work depend on the actual run. Electron smoke test · Go collaboration tests · Release workflow

articles.title: FastMRZ 3 - Passport MRZ Extraction in Pure Python, No Tesseract
articles.description: If you have ever built KYC onboarding, hotel check-in or border-control software, you know the MRZ: the two or three lines of <<<-padded text at the bottom of a passport, ID card or visa. Reading it sounds simple. It is 37 possible characters (A-Z, 0-9 and <) in a fixed layout defined by ICAO 9303. In practice, most Python MRZ tools come with the same setup ritual: Install Tesseract at system level Download a special MRZ traineddata file Copy it into the correct tessdata folder Make sure all of that also exists in your Docker image, Lambda layer, CI runner and the Windows laptop of whoever joins the team next And after all that, it still struggles with phone photos that are skewed, blurred or badly lit. The first versions of FastMRZ had the same problem, because they used Tesseract under the hood. With FastMRZ 3, I removed Tesseract completely. What's new in FastMRZ 3 No Tesseract. FastMRZ now ships its own ONNX text recogniser, trained only for the MRZ character set. Pure Python install. The only dependencies are numpy, opencv-python-headless and pymupdf. No system packages, no traineddata files. More accurate than the Tesseract-based versions, because the recogniser only has to tell apart 37 characters in one fixed font, not every glyph in every language. More input types. File paths, NumPy arrays, Base64 strings, raw bytes, PDFs and plain MRZ text. Batch processing in parallel. More document formats. TD1, TD2, TD3, MRV-A and MRV-B. Install pip install fastmrz That's the whole setup. Quick start from fastmrz import FastMRZ fast_mrz = FastMRZ() details = fast_mrz.get_details("passport.jpg") print(details) Output (trimmed): status is SUCCESS only when the format and every ICAO 9303 check digit are valid. Otherwise it is FAILURE, and status_message tells you the first problem found. If no MRZ is found in the image at all, you get: No exceptions to catch, no silent garbage. Either the data passed the checksums or you're told why it didn't. Every input type you'll actually use In real systems, images rarely arrive as files on disk. They come from an upload endpoint, a camera frame or a scanned PDF. FastMRZ takes all of them: # Raw MRZ text instead of parsed fields text = fast_mrz.get_details("passport.jpg", ignore_parse=True) # OpenCV / camera frame (BGR or grayscale ndarray) details = fast_mrz.get_details(image_array, input_type="numpy") # From a web or mobile client details = fast_mrz.get_details(b64_string, input_type="base64") # Straight from an upload or S3 object details = fast_mrz.get_details(image_bytes, input_type="bytes") # Scanned PDF - uses the first page with an MRZ details = fast_mrz.get_details("scan.pdf", input_type="pdf") # Already have the MRZ string? Parse and validate only details = fast_mrz.get_details(mrz_string, input_type="text") Two more helpers: # Check digits only result = fast_mrz.validate_mrz(mrz_string) # {"is_valid": ..., "status_message": ...} # Get the rectified MRZ crop, useful for audit logs or manual review strip = fast_mrz.get_mrz_image("passport.jpg") Batch processing results = fast_mrz.get_details_batch(["a.jpg", "b.jpg", "c.jpg"]) Results come back in input order Runs in parallel. workers defaults to your CPU count, capped at 8 Expect roughly 1.5x the throughput of a plain loop on a 4-core CPU A file that can't be read doesn't stop the batch. Its entry just comes back as FAILURE with a message It takes the same options as get_details: get_details_batch(inputs, input_type="imagepath", ignore_parse=False, include_checkdigit=True, workers=None) How it works Locate. OpenCV contour detection plus an ONNX model find the MRZ region, even when the document isn't perfectly aligned in the photo. Rectify. The MRZ strip is cropped, deskewed and normalised. Recognise. A small ONNX model reads the characters. Because it only has to handle the 37 MRZ symbols in the OCR-B font, it can be far smaller and more reliable on this job than a general-purpose OCR engine. Validate. Every check digit defined by ICAO 9303 is verified, and the fields are parsed into clean, structured output. Everything runs locally on CPU. No document image ever leaves your machine, which matters when you're handling passports. Supported documents Format Used on Lines x chars TD1 ID cards 3 x 30 TD2 Older ID cards, some visas 2 x 36 TD3 Passports 2 x 44 MRV-A Visas (large) MRV-B Visas (small) Migrating from PassportEye # PassportEye from passporteye import read_mrz mrz = read_mrz("passport.jpg") data = mrz.to_dict() # FastMRZ data = FastMRZ().get_details("passport.jpg") No Tesseract install, and the status field tells you whether the checksums passed. Upgrading from FastMRZ 1.x / 2.x Remove Tesseract from your Dockerfile and setup scripts. You no longer need it. If you still pass the old tesseract_path or tessdata_path arguments, FastMRZ 3 ignores them and raises a FutureWarning, so you can clean them up at your own pace. Where it fits KYC and customer onboarding in banking and fintech Hotel, airline and car-rental check-in Travel, immigration and visa processing Any back-office workflow where staff type passport details by hand today Try it, break it, tell me GitHub: https://github.com/sivakumar-mahalingam/fastmrz PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/fastmrz/ FastMRZ is open source under Apache-2.0. The most useful thing you can send me is a failure case. If FastMRZ can't read one of your documents, open an issue with a redacted sample and I'll use it to improve the model. And if it saves you a Tesseract install, a star on GitHub helps other developers find it.

articles.title: The Strategic Executive vs. the Tactical Executive
articles.description: In technology leadership, the difference between a tactical executive and a strategic executive is not simply a matter of style. It reflects two different ways of understanding problems, making decisions, and creating value for the organization. The tactical executive focuses primarily on immediate actions and technical details. When a security incident occurs, for example, this leader may concentrate on identifying the vulnerability, applying the patch, and restoring the system. This response can be necessary, especially during a crisis, because tactical execution provides speed, control, and short-term stability. However, the tactical executive often remains focused on the symptoms of a problem. The discussion may center on the specific bug, the system failure, or the operational task that needs to be completed. Although this approach can solve the immediate issue, it may not address the organizational or governance gap that allowed the problem to happen in the first place. The strategic executive, by contrast, looks beyond the immediate event. After a security incident, this leader does not spend most of the discussion explaining the technical details of the patch. Instead, the strategic executive asks what the incident revealed about the company’s processes, security practices, governance, and risk exposure. The focus shifts from “How did we fix the problem?” to “How can we prevent this type of problem from happening again?” This distinction can also be seen in communication with the board. A tactical technology executive may present engineering activities such as completed tasks, merged pull requests, or infrastructure changes. A strategic executive translates those activities into business outcomes. Instead of saying that the company needs to modernize its architecture, the strategic leader explains that the current system is delaying revenue-generating features, increasing costs, or limiting the company’s ability to compete. The tactical executive typically sees technology through the lens of capability and execution. The strategic executive sees it through the lens of risk, return, and competitive advantage. For the strategic leader, technology is not an end in itself. It is a means of increasing revenue, reducing costs, protecting the company, improving scalability, and creating a stronger position in the market. This strategic perspective offers several important advantages. First, it improves decision-making. When technical investments are connected to business priorities, the board and senior leadership can evaluate them more effectively. They can understand not only what a project costs, but also what value it may create and what risks it may reduce. Second, strategic leadership improves resource allocation. A strategic executive can show how engineering capacity is divided among innovation, growth, scale, and maintenance. This makes trade-offs visible. For example, dedicating more resources to security may temporarily reduce feature development, but it can also protect revenue, customer trust, and regulatory compliance. Third, strategic executives build greater trust. They do not hide behind technical language or present themselves as heroes who personally solve every problem. Instead, they describe the strengths and weaknesses of the engineering system. Successes are connected to scalable processes, while failures are treated as systemic gaps that the organization must address. Finally, strategic leadership gives technology a stronger role in the future of the company. A strategic executive can identify technical capabilities that may improve the organization’s competitive position over the next twelve to eighteen months. The focus is not on adopting technology because it is fashionable, but on understanding how it can accelerate growth, reduce the cost of scaling, or improve the company’s ability to innovate. Being tactical is not inherently negative. Tactical execution is essential for responding to incidents, delivering projects, and maintaining daily operations. The limitation arises when a leader remains exclusively tactical and never connects immediate actions to broader business consequences. The most effective technology executives are capable of operating tactically when necessary while thinking strategically at all times. They can understand the technical details, but they do not allow those details to dominate the conversation. Their responsibility is to transform complexity into clarity and technical activity into business value. In the end, the strategic executive is more than a manager of systems and teams. This leader becomes a partner in defining priorities, allocating capital, managing risk, and shaping the company’s future. That is why strategic thinking is one of the most important qualities a technology executive can develop.

articles.title: The Swap Is Only the Beginning: 5 Things That Happen Between Your Wallet and a TRON Transaction
articles.description: TronSeven — Non-Custodial Token Swaps on TRON Network Swap TRC-20 tokens on TRON with self-custody and open-source smart contracts. Low fees, verifiable on TRONSCAN. tronseven.com A practical look at wallet permissions, smart contracts, network resources, and what users should understand before exchanging TRON tokens. You select two tokens. You enter an amount. You connect your wallet. You press Swap. A few seconds later, the transaction appears on the blockchain. It sounds simple. And from a user's perspective, it should be. But underneath that clean interface is a sequence of technical operations that deserves more attention than it usually gets. A crypto swap is not just a conversion between two numbers. It is an interaction between a wallet, a smart contract, token permissions, network resources, and blockchain settlement. Understanding those moving parts can help users make better decisions, avoid unnecessary mistakes, and evaluate swap platforms more intelligently. Let's break it down using the TRON ecosystem as our example. Your wallet is more than a place to store tokens A common misconception is that connecting a wallet means handing control of your cryptocurrency to an application. These are two very different things. A wallet is the interface through which you manage your keys and authorize blockchain interactions. A non-custodial application should allow you to interact with smart contracts without taking possession of your assets. That distinction matters. Before using any swap service, ask yourself: Does the application require you to deposit funds into an account? Can you inspect the contract receiving your transaction? Does the wallet clearly display the action you are approving? Are you being asked to sign something unrelated to the swap? Never approve a wallet request simply because a website tells you to. Your private keys and recovery phrase should remain private. A legitimate swap interface should never need your seed phrase. Token approval and token exchange are not necessarily the same operation This is one of the most important concepts in smart-contract-based token exchanges. Many TRC-20 tokens implement an allowance mechanism. In simple terms, a token holder can authorize a particular smart contract to spend a specified amount of tokens on their behalf. This is commonly handled through an approval transaction. Why does this matter? Because approving a token allowance and executing a swap are conceptually different actions. An approval establishes permission. A swap executes an exchange according to the relevant contract logic. Users should understand what allowance they are granting, which contract receives it, and whether the requested amount is reasonable. This is particularly important when interacting with unfamiliar decentralized applications. A good habit is to review permissions rather than treating every wallet confirmation as an ordinary login. TRON network resources are part of the transaction experience TRON has a resource model that includes Bandwidth and Energy. These resources are used when transactions are processed on the network. Bandwidth relates primarily to transaction data, while Energy is associated with the computational work required to execute smart contracts. This creates an interesting difference between simply transferring a token and interacting with a more complex smart contract. For users, the practical question is straightforward: What will this transaction actually cost me? The answer can depend on available network resources, the contract operation, and the transaction's execution requirements. This is why looking only at the advertised exchange rate is not enough. A useful swap interface should make transaction costs understandable before the user confirms the operation. The displayed exchange rate is only one part of the decision Imagine exchanging USDT for another TRC-20 asset. You see a quote that looks attractive. Should you immediately confirm? Not necessarily. There are several things worth checking: Exchange rate: How much of the receiving asset is estimated for your input? Price impact: Could your trade size affect the execution price? Liquidity: Is there sufficient liquidity for the selected token pair? Network costs: What resources are required to execute the transaction? Minimum received: Is there protection against receiving substantially less than expected? These details help explain why two swap interfaces can present different experiences even when they support the same blockchain. A better approach is to compare the complete transaction rather than focusing on one attractive number. Blockchain transparency should be something users can actually verify One of the strongest properties of public blockchains is that transactions can be independently inspected. You do not have to rely entirely on a platform's marketing description. On TRON, TRONSCAN provides a way to investigate transactions, addresses, and smart-contract activity. This is an important part of evaluating any swap application. Look for: A publicly identifiable smart-contract address. Contract source code and verification information. Transaction records that can be inspected independently. Clear documentation explaining how the application works. An audit or security review can be useful evidence, but it is not a guarantee that a system is risk-free. Users should still examine the available information and understand the risks associated with smart-contract interactions. Where does TronSeven fit into this picture? These principles become much more interesting when applied to an actual TRON-native swap application. One project worth examining is TronSeven. Website: https://tronseven.com TronSeven presents itself as a non-custodial exchange focused on TRON assets, including TRX and TRC-20 tokens such as USDT and USDC. The platform lists wallet connectivity through: TronLink Trust Wallet WalletConnect It also provides publicly accessible smart-contract information and a TRONSCAN link, giving users a starting point for independently investigating its on-chain infrastructure. Another interesting aspect is its approach to network resources. The project describes using TRON Energy to cover swap-related network costs. Rather than evaluating a swap platform solely by its interface, users can examine these technical details and decide whether its approach fits their requirements. You can explore the application and its published information here: https://tronseven.com A simple checklist before your next TRON swap Before confirming an exchange, take a moment to review these points: Network: Are both assets on the correct blockchain? Token contract: Have you checked that you selected the intended token? Wallet: Is the application requesting only the permissions necessary for the operation? Allowance: Do you understand which contract is authorized to spend your tokens? Quote: Have you reviewed the expected receiving amount and price impact? Resources: Do you understand the potential network costs? Verification: Can you inspect the relevant contract and transaction information? This checklist takes less time than recovering from a transaction made without understanding what you approved. Final thoughts: Better swaps begin with better understanding The TRON ecosystem continues to offer practical opportunities for people using stablecoins, decentralized applications, and TRC-20 assets. But a good swap experience should involve more than a convenient button. It should combine understandable transaction details, clear wallet interactions, transparent smart-contract information, and a process users can independently investigate. That's the perspective worth bringing to every exchange. If you're exploring TRON-native token swaps, take a closer look at TronSeven, examine its available contract information, and see how its swap interface works. What WooCommerce Automation Really Costs (Build, Tools and AI)
articles.description: Store owners usually ask what the tool costs. The better question is what the whole project costs over a year. Here is how I break down automation around WooCommerce. Build cost by tier These are planning ranges based on typical freelance work, not fixed quotes. Tier What you get Range Starter One or two workflows, such as order alerts and a spreadsheet log $300 to $800 Standard Four to eight workflows, error alerts, retries, documentation $800 to $2,500 Advanced Custom APIs, AI features, CRM or accounting sync, approvals $2,500 to $8,000+ Cost follows hours, not tools. At roughly $40 to $90 an hour, a Starter build is 6 to 12 hours and a Standard build 15 to 40. What raises the hours is rarely the first connection. It is refunds, partial shipments, failed payments, missing data and retries after an outage. Zapier, Make or n8n All three can listen to WooCommerce events through webhooks and the REST API. They bill differently, which is where surprises come from. Zapier: fastest setup, free tier, paid plans from roughly $20 to $30 a month. Every step counts as a task, so long workflows get expensive. Make: free tier, entry plans around $10 a month. Counts operations per step. n8n: cloud plans from about $20 a month, or self-hosted on a small server for roughly $5 to $20 a month, plus the time to maintain and secure it. Prices change often, so check each pricing page. Before you commit, multiply the steps in a workflow by your monthly orders to see what the platform will really charge. Where AI fits AI helps when a workflow has to read text: support triage, drafting replies, product descriptions for review, summarising reviews. It is not needed for rules like "notify the manager above a certain order total", and plain rules are cheaper and more predictable. AI providers bill by usage. For a small or mid-sized store that is often a few dollars to tens of dollars a month, but it depends on volume, so set a monthly cap. Keep a person in the loop for prices, refunds and anything legal. Low-risk tasks like tagging can run on their own. Does it pay back? Say six hours a week of order entry, shipping emails and stock checks at $25 an hour. That is about $7,800 a year. A $1,200 build plus $40 a month in tools costs about $1,680 in year one, so the build is recovered in roughly eight to ten weeks. If the task takes thirty minutes a week, it will not pay back for a long time. Leave it alone. Risks to budget for Duplicate actions when a workflow runs twice Silent failures with no error alert API changes that need an occasional fix Customer data passing through every connected service Testing on the live store instead of a staging copy FAQ Do I need AI for store automation? No. Order alerts, stock warnings and tracking emails are rule-based and need no AI. Can automation break my store? A badly built workflow can send duplicate emails or miss orders, but it does not change the store itself. Build on a copy, test refunds and set error alerts. Who should own the workflows? You. They should live in your own platform accounts, with documentation. Large log records in Dynatrace: limits, native support and best practices
articles.description: A ticket lands: « the partner call is cut off halfway through in the logs ». You open the record and it simply stops. The payload crossed a limit somewhere. Large log records in Dynatrace raise exactly this operational question: how big can a record be, and on which path? This article starts from that decision (keep, split or shrink a record) and checks every figure against the official documentation, read on 12 November 2026. It applies to Dynatrace SaaS (Grail and OpenPipeline). I did not verify Dynatrace Managed limits for this piece, so I quote none. If cost is a new topic for you, read log costs: ingest, retain and query first. The typical case: a record of several hundred kilobytes A billing XML message, a partner API’s JSON response, a stack trace with its full context: such events quickly grow past a kilobyte. The vendor’s post puts this range between a few hundred kilobytes and several megabytes. For a long time the default answer was to truncate or split upstream, at the price of lost context. The same post announces native support for single log events of up to 10 MB, with no configuration, through OneAgent, OpenTelemetry, the API or other collectors. It is vendor presentation material: it does not say what happens above 10 MB. The reference documentation spells out the conditions. Large log records in Dynatrace: the limits to check The Log Management and Analytics default limits page gives these values: Log entry body (content): 10 MB, but only 512 kB for logs processed by the Classic pipeline. API request: 10 MB at the endpoint; a batch above 16 MB after preprocessing is rejected with HTTP 413. Records per request: 50,000. Attributes: 500 per log, attribute value capped at 32 kB, key at 100 bytes, 5 levels of nested objects. Size after processing in OpenPipeline: 16 MB, according to the OpenPipeline limits page. Keep the first line in mind: « 10 MB » is not a universal promise. The Classic path stays at 512 kB. If a long log vanishes or stops short, check which pipeline it goes through first. This capture is the real output of commands run on a test file. The 600,000-byte record exceeds the Classic limit but stays far below 10 MB. Send a big record and check its size Here is how to test on a pre-production environment. Create an API token with the log ingest scope and keep it in an environment variable. Build a JSON file with a large content field. Send it with curl to the ingest API and note the status code. Query the logs in DQL to measure the length of the content received. fetch logs | filter log.source == "payment-gateway" | fieldsAdd size = stringLength(content) | sort size desc | limit 10 A 204 means everything was accepted. The documentation also lists 400 or 200 depending on whether all or some events fall outside the accepted time range. If the measured size is below what you sent, a limit cut the content: go back to the list above. For syntax, see log pattern analysis. What to do with a huge log once ingested A multi-megabyte record costs storage, queries and reading time. Ask three questions in this order: Who reads it? If nobody reads the whole body, extract the useful fields (error code, order ID) and keep the rest for investigations. Which part is sensitive? A big JSON often hides personal data. See masking in OpenPipeline. Which pipeline fits? Route these logs to a dedicated pipeline with its own rules: create and route a pipeline. Watch two processing limits. An extracted attribute is truncated to 4,096 characters when added to the event template. Each DQL processor script is limited to 8,192 characters, according to the OpenPipeline limits page. Best practices Measure the real size of your biggest events before changing anything. Confirm the pipeline (Classic or OpenPipeline) of every source that produces big logs. Do not use logs to carry files: a log is an event, not storage. Extract useful fields at ingest and drop the rest when you can. Test a send above the limit in pre-production to learn the real behaviour: the documentation I read does not describe it for every path. Frequently asked questions What is the maximum log size in Dynatrace? According to the SaaS documentation, an entry body can reach 10 MB, but only 512 kB on the Classic pipeline. Check the limits page before committing, as it changes. Should I split large logs before sending them? Not necessarily on the 10 MB path, according to the vendor’s post. On the Classic pipeline the 512 kB limit still applies. Measure with the DQL query above. Does this apply to Dynatrace Managed? This article covers SaaS only. For Managed, read the Managed documentation and do not reuse these figures. Conclusion Large log records in Dynatrace pass up to 10 MB on the Grail path, but the Classic pipeline cuts at 512 kB: the incident at the top often comes down to that detail. Measure, route, extract. Sources: Log Management and Analytics default limits, OpenPipeline limits, and the vendor post on large log records. span.observer is an independent community blog, not affiliated with Dynatrace LLC.
