articles.title: ESP32-P4 boot loop (CHIP_LP_WDT_RESET): building a homelab watchdog in ESPHome
articles.description: My homelab's monitoring has a daft weak spot. Uptime Kuma runs on my NAS. So if the NAS goes down, the thing that's meant to tell me the NAS is down goes with it. I've got a script on another box that restarts Kuma if it dies, but that's still the homelab watching itself. So I bought a Waveshare ESP32-P4-ETH. Wired Ethernet, can run off PoE, no WiFi at all. My first idea was to move Uptime Kuma onto it. That was never happening, it's a microcontroller, not a Linux box. So on 13 October 2026 I settled on something it can actually do: be a small, dumb, independent watchdog that doesn't rely on any of my servers to send an alert. What it does Every 60 seconds it checks 10 things: Uptime Kuma, SSH on the NAS, the reverse proxy, both Proxmox nodes, my agent box, Vaultwarden, the router's web page, AdGuard DNS, and the internet (1.1.1.1:443). Most of those are just a TCP connect. DNS is a proper one: it builds a real A-record query for cloudflare.com by hand and sends it straight at AdGuard, then checks the answer has the right ID, no error and at least one record. An open port doesn't mean DNS is working. 3 failures in a row and it posts 🔴 DOWN to Discord, straight from the board. The first good check after that posts 🟢 RECOVERED with how many minutes it was down. Three strikes stops one dropped packet waking me up. If it can't send (say the internet's gone), the alert goes in a queue. It keeps the newest 20 and retries every cycle. Every cycle it also pushes to an Uptime Kuma push monitor with a 120 second heartbeat. So Kuma watches the board while the board watches Kuma. If either dies, the other one says so. All the checks run in their own FreeRTOS task, so a target that hangs on connect never blocks the rest of the board. I wrote it as ESPHome YAML plus one C++ header. ESPHome gives me OTA updates, a web page and the Ethernet setup for free, and the header does the actual checking. Compile trap: socket() is ambiguous First compile failed on something stupid. ESPHome has its own esphome::socket namespace, so a bare socket() call inside my code was ambiguous. You have to use the global ones: ::socket, ::connect, ::close and so on. After that it compiled clean. RAM 13.5%, flash 695 KB. Tiny. The boot loop I flashed it from my Mac late on 13 October and it went straight into a boot loop. Reset every 3.2 seconds or so, no app log at all, just this: rst:0x10 (CHIP_LP_WDT_RESET) No app log means it's dying before my code even runs, so it wasn't my watchdog code. It was the build. I'd copied board: esp32-p4-evboard because that's what you'd reach for. Turns out in ESPHome that board means the engineering sample P4, the pre-production chips before revision 3. My board has a production chip, revision v3.2. So the firmware was built for the wrong silicon, and the chip's low-power watchdog reset it every few seconds. The fix was to stop naming a board at all and just tell ESPHome the chip: esp32: variant: esp32p4 engineering_sample: false cpu_frequency: 360MHZ # 400MHz on the P4 is marked experimental in ESPHome flash_size: 16MB framework: type: esp-idf That set the minimum chip revision to 3.1 in the build config, and it booted fine. If you've got a P4 board in a boot loop with CHIP_LP_WDT_RESET and no log, check you're not building for the engineering sample. The first live flash sent nothing anywhere On 15 October it went on the network for real. Kuma push: 404. Discord: 400. The OTA password was, word for word, REPLACE-with-a-long-random-string. Yeah. The first flash had used the example secrets file with the placeholders still in. Nothing was broken, it just had nothing real to talk to. I rebuilt with proper secrets and pushed it over OTA, then checked the old placeholder password got rejected and the new one got accepted. One false "heartbeat DOWN" from Kuma went out while the old firmware was still running, which fair enough, it wasn't sending real heartbeats. While I'm on secrets: esphome config prints your Discord webhook in full, because it ends up inside a lambda. Don't paste that output anywhere. Two false alarms that were actually right Once it was talking, it straight away said two things were DOWN: SSH on the NAS and the router's web page. Both were fine from my laptop. The board was right though. I'd plugged it into a router port that's on my IoT VLAN, so it got an IoT address. And my IoT VLAN isn't allowed to reach NAS SSH or the router's admin page. That's the firewall doing its job. I moved that router port over to the main LAN, bounced the port so it asked for a new address, and it picked up its reserved one. 10 out of 10 up, and it posted RECOVERED for both. Kuma's ping monitor for it went green too. Worth saying: a watchdog that sits on a different network from the thing it watches is testing the firewall, not the service. Put it where your users are. What I added after A password on its web page. sieve, my own vulnerability scanner, flagged the open web UI, so it's behind a login now. An off-site dead-man switch. The board can tell me a server is down, but if the power goes or the internet drops, nothing at home can tell me anything. So I've got a free Cloudflare Worker that expects check-ins and posts to Discord if they stop for 5 minutes. Two of my servers already pinged it every minute, and since 16 October the watchdog does too, every cycle. That one's got its own story (the cron trigger didn't fire at first), I'll write it up separately. How it's doing This is the board's own state, read off its web page on 18 October 2026: 2,061 check cycles, about 34 hours since its last restart, nothing down, nothing stuck in the queue. Not much to look at, which is the point. If you're building one On a production ESP32-P4, use variant: esp32p4 and engineering_sample: false, not the evboard. In ESPHome C++ code, call ::socket and friends with the :: in front. Check something real for DNS, not just the port. Put the board on the same network as whoever uses the services, or you're testing the firewall. Have something off-site for the power cut case, because the board goes off with everything else. What watches your monitoring? I genuinely didn't have an answer to that until this month. 🤖 Drafted with AI assistance from my own homelab notes, logs and repos, and fact-checked against them before publishing.

articles.title: Two Agents, Two Definitions of 'Done': The Contract to Write Before You Wire Them Together
articles.description: The failure mode nobody writes about: two AI agents, both running, both "up" on every dashboard — and the job quietly not getting done. On the November 11 episode of The Cognitive Revolution, Vijoy Pandey — SVP and GM of Outshift by Cisco, the incubation arm that has deployed multi-agent systems with Swisscom, ServiceNow, SoftServe, and Webex — described a gap that standard monitoring never shows. In Cisco's own five-agent deployments, accuracy fell from 99% with no misalignments between the agents to 16% with three. In one travel-booking test, the system was mostly up and connected while completing zero tasks. And in an analysis of public ChatDev sessions, Cisco reported semantic or cognitive-misalignment failures in 100% of the sessions it examined. "Connectivity is not the same as cognition," Pandey told host Nathan Labenz. "What we need to move towards is shared cognition and shared reasoning." His diagnosis: the industry measures whether agents are up and connected, while agents can be connected and still not understand each other. The value, he argued, is not in any one agent — "the value is actually in the handoff that's happening between these agents." The failure isn't capability. It's vocabulary. Most multi-agent advice focuses on architecture: which agent does what, who orchestrates, how they connect. The failure Pandey described is duller and more dangerous: two competent agents that mean different things by the same word. At small-business scale, the version looks like this: Your sales agent marks a job "done" when the customer accepts the quote. Your invoicing agent considers the job "done" when payment clears. Your sales agent calls someone a "customer" the moment they sign. Your billing system calls them a "customer" only once an invoice exists. Both definitions are defensible. Neither agent is broken. But the moment you wire automation across that seam — sales closes the job, invoicing starts billing — you have two different meanings of the trigger word routing real money. The handoff fires early, or late, or on the wrong population, and everything looks green while it happens. Cisco's answer was to open-source three protocols, which Outshift describes as observe, align, and validate: Scope builds knowledge graphs on agent traces to find cognitive failures; Accord has agents agree on intent, scope, key terms, and the definition of "done" before work starts; Concord has agents negotiate an outcome every one can accept when they disagree. You do not need to install any of that. You need the idea underneath it: the definitions get written down before the wiring, not after the failure. The handoff contract: one page, 20 minutes Before you connect any two agents — or an agent to a system it will trigger — write five fields. One page per seam; a three-agent setup has three seams, and each gets its own page. 1. Name the pair. "Sales agent → invoicing agent." Every contract covers exactly two systems. If a diagram is forming in your head, you're overcomplicating it — the contract is pairwise, not a hub. 2. List the words that cross the seam. Not every word — the load-bearing nouns, usually five or fewer: done, customer, paid, urgent, late. Pull the actual messages that will pass between the two systems and highlight the words both sides will act on. 3. Write each side's current definition. One line each, no editing, no fixing yet. Done (sales agent): quote accepted, kickoff email sent. Done (invoicing agent): invoice issued, payment reconciled. The differences are usually obvious the moment they're on paper — which is exactly why they need to be on paper. 4. Negotiate the shared definition. Where the two sides differ, write the one definition both will use — and make it checkable. "Done = quote accepted AND kickoff email sent AND invoice issued" is a definition an agent can test. "Done = the customer is taken care of" is a vibe. This is Accord's job shrunk to a paragraph. 5. Write the conflict rule. When a message arrives that doesn't fit the shared definitions, the receiving agent stops and asks a human. Never improvise a meaning. This is Concord's negotiation step shrunk to its SMB version: escalate, don't guess. The 99%-to-16% collapse came from misalignments that went uncorrected — the contract's job is to catch the collision while it's still a question, not a loss. Then run one real past case through the seam before you turn the wiring on — the trickiest one from last month. If the two agents don't classify it identically against the contract, the contract isn't finished. Where this fails (the honest list) A contract fixes collisions, not competence. Perfect definitions make two agents agree; they don't make either one good. If the model writes a bad email, the contract just ensures both agents agree it was sent. Sometimes the answer is one agent. If a single agent can do the whole job end to end, do that and skip the seam entirely. Contracts are for handoffs you actually need — don't create a second agent just to have something to wire. The numbers are a warning, not a benchmark. The 99%-to-16% collapse and the 100% ChatDev figure come from Cisco's own deployments and its analysis of public sessions. They establish the failure mode exists, not your odds of hitting it. Even the builders haven't finished. Pandey reported on the same episode that his own personal agent and his wife's — each carrying one identity across several models — still struggle to coordinate on their humans' behalf, down to booking a shared dinner. If the executive open-sourcing alignment protocols is still working on it, a one-page contract doesn't put you behind. It puts you ahead of most of the market. Where to start You can't write a handoff contract for agents you don't know you're running. Shadow usage means most small businesses already have two AI tools touching the same customers without anyone writing down what happens between them — one paid by the company, one installed by an employee, no shared definitions anywhere. That's the first thing the AI Clarity Sprint maps: every AI touchpoint in your business — paid tools, AI features inside software you already own, and the employee shadow usage nobody approved — in two weeks, for one fixed fee ($1,495 CAD). You finish with the complete inventory, the seams worth writing contracts for, and a ranked plan for what to do first. The cheapest place to fix a misalignment is before the wiring. The second cheapest is the week you find the seam.

articles.title: Shipping AI-Ready (/llms.txt + MCP) & EAA/WCAG 2.2 Compliant Sites on Craft CMS 4 & 5
articles.description: Agencies building content-rich sites on Craft CMS 4 and Craft CMS 5 love Craft for a clear reason: clean Twig templates, custom Entry types, Matrix/CKEditor flexibility, and zero opinionated frontend markup forced onto your design system. In 2026, however, two new technical specifications have landed on almost every agency launch checklist: AI Search & Agent Readiness (GEO): Ensuring OAI-SearchBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot, and autonomous MCP agents receive clean Markdown, /llms.txt Section indexes, and Schema.org graphs rather than 350 KB of layout chrome. European Accessibility Act (EAA / EN 301 549) & WCAG 2.2 AA: Preventing content editors from accidentally publishing inaccessible HTML or untagged scanned PDF attachments. Here is how to implement both cleanly inside Craft's Yii2 event lifecycle without bloating your Twig templates. 1. Serving /llms.txt and Accept: text/markdown in Craft CMS Instead of scattering custom routes across every project's config/routes.php, a Craft plugin can listen to WebApplication::EVENT_BEFORE_REQUEST and Response::EVENT_AFTER_PREPARE: /llms.txt & /llms-full.txt: Query active Craft Sections and published Entry::find()->status('live') elements per site handle, outputting a deterministic Markdown sitemap with canonical URLs and summaries. HTTP Content Negotiation (Accept: text/markdown): When an AI retrieval bot sends Accept: text/markdown, convert / semantic HTML into token-efficient Markdown and attach Vary: Accept plus Link: ; rel="llms-txt" headers so CDN caches (Cloudflare, Fastly) never mix HTML and Markdown responses. MCP & Google A2A Discovery Cards: Expose /.well-known/mcp/server-card.json and /.well-known/agent.json so AI agents can query published Entries through a read-only JSON endpoint rather than scraping HTML pagination. You can benchmark how your live Craft, Joomla, WordPress, or OpenCart domain responds to these 25 protocol checks in 3 seconds using the free FlexExt AI Website Checker. 2. Automated EAA / WCAG 2.2 Guardrails & PDF/UA Auditing Passing a WCAG 2.2 AA audit on launch day is only half the battle — two weeks later, an editor uploads a scanned PDF brochure without /StructTreeRoot tags or skips from straight to inside a CKEditor field. By hooking into Craft's element save lifecycle and Asset volumes, automated guardrails can inspect: Missing alt attributes, empty links/buttons, missing table headers, and skipped H1–H6 heading levels. articles.title: Windows Hello and BitLocker PINs: the flash chip attack on TPM lockout
articles.description: Originally published at coinetic.io. A short PIN is safe on Windows for one reason: after a few wrong guesses the TPM security chip makes you wait, so nobody can try all 10,000 four-digit PINs. Researchers at TU Berlin have shown that on some PCs this waiting can be undone by someone who opens the device and wires into the flash chip on the mainboard. This page explains what that means for your laptop, and the few settings that make it far harder. Why now: the "Hello Again" research (November 2026) What: the TPM in many PCs is built into the processor's firmware (a firmware TPM) and keeps its state, including the count of wrong PINs, in a flash chip on the mainboard. The researchers found that a Winbond flash chip can be made to leak its key by voltage glitching, and that AMD's firmware did not check that the counter in the flash really went up. Together this lets an attacker roll the TPM state back and keep guessing. Effect, per the paper: worst case for a 4-digit Windows Hello PIN drops from about 69 days to about 40 hours; for a 6-digit BitLocker startup PIN (TPM + PIN) from about 19 years to about 20 days. Longer PINs remain out of reach for practical purposes. Needs: the device itself, opened, with hardware attached to the mainboard. It is not a remote attack. No attacks outside the research lab were known at publication. Vendors: AMD tracks its part as CVE-2026-43613 (bulletin AMD-SB-7079) and is shipping firmware updates for affected processors from November 2026 into February 2027. According to reports, Microsoft rated the Windows Hello report moderate, did not assign a Windows CVE and recommends PINs of at least six digits; Intel says the flash chip used is the deciding factor; Winbond says a fix needs a new chip design. Sources: Research paper "Hello Again" (TU Berlin) · AMD security bulletin AMD-SB-7079 · Born's Tech and Windows World (German) In short Install firmware (BIOS / UEFI) updates from your PC maker as they arrive – that is where AMD's fix comes from, not from Windows Update alone. Make the PIN longer: at least 8 digits, or letters and digits. Every extra digit multiplies the attacker's work by ten. For BitLocker with a startup PIN: allow enhanced (alphanumeric) PINs and set a longer minimum length. Keep the device with you, and have a plan for a lost or stolen laptop: who to tell, which accounts to lock, which access to revoke. A firewall cannot stop a physical attack on a stolen laptop. It can keep your other computers from being opened with what is on that laptop. 1. What the attack does – in plain words Your Windows Hello PIN is not a password the attacker can test on another computer. It only works on this device, and the TPM chip counts wrong guesses and locks for a while after too many. That lockout is what makes a 4-digit PIN acceptable. The attack does not break the PIN or the encryption. It cheats the counter: the attacker saves the TPM's state from the flash chip, tries a few PINs, then puts the old state back so the TPM "forgets" the wrong guesses. Repeat until the PIN is found. With the PIN, the attacker can sign in to that laptop as you, use the keys Windows Hello protects (for example single sign-on to your company's cloud services from that device), and with a BitLocker startup PIN, unlock the disk. What it needs: your laptop, a screwdriver, soldering or clip-on wiring to the flash chip, and time – hours to days for a short PIN. This is a risk for a stolen or seized device, not for a PC that stays in your hands. 2. Is my PC affected? The research targets firmware TPMs that keep their state in the mainboard flash: AMD systems, and PCs with Winbond flash chips of the type examined, whatever the processor. Whether a given model is affected depends on processor and flash chip – watch your PC maker's security advisories. See which TPM you have: press Windows+R, type tpm.msc, Enter, and look at Manufacturer Name. Or in PowerShell: Get-Tpm | Select-Object ManufacturerIdTxt, ManufacturerVersion. AMD means the firmware TPM of an AMD processor. Desktops in a locked office are a smaller concern than laptops that travel. Rank by how easily a device can be taken away. 3. Updates first Firmware updates: AMD delivers its fix in processor firmware, which reaches you as a BIOS / UEFI update from your PC maker (HP, Lenovo, Dell, Framework and others). Use the maker's update tool or Windows Update's optional driver and firmware updates. Managed fleets: check your maker's advisory list for the models you own. Windows updates as usual. The firmware update does not replace a longer PIN: the research also covers flash chips for which no software fix exists. 4. Make the PIN longer The lockout was the only thing protecting short PINs. Without it, length is what counts. The researchers recommend adding at least two digits, or using eight or more. On your own PC Settings › Accounts › Sign-in options › PIN (Windows Hello) › Change PIN. Choose at least 8 digits – or tick Include letters and symbols, which makes guessing many times harder. In a company (Group Policy or Intune) Windows Hello PIN: Computer Configuration › Administrative Templates › System › PIN Complexity › Minimum PIN length (with newer templates also under Windows Components › Windows Hello for Business). Set at least 6, better 8. In Intune: Endpoint security › Account protection, or the Windows Hello for Business settings in the enrollment policy. Check after the rollout that users really have changed short PINs. BitLocker startup PIN: Computer Configuration › Administrative Templates › Windows Components › BitLocker Drive Encryption › Operating System Drives: Allow enhanced PINs for startup (letters and symbols) and Configure minimum PIN length for startup. Users then change their PIN with manage-bde -changepin C: as administrator. 5. Second-line defences for a lost or stolen device Report and revoke quickly: the attack takes time. If a laptop is missing, disable or delete the device in Entra ID / Intune, revoke the user's sessions, rotate the BitLocker recovery key, and reset the user's password. At home: change the password of your Microsoft account and sign out other devices from it. Remote wipe where you use Intune or another device management: a wiped device has nothing left to unlock. Do not rely on the device alone for access to important systems: require multi-factor sign-in with a second device (phone, security key) for VPN, remote access and admin accounts. Physical care: do not leave laptops in cars or hotel rooms; tamper-evident seals help notice an opened case. 6. What Coinetic AI Security can and cannot do here Honestly first: Coinetic AI Security manages the Windows Firewall. A firewall does not stop someone who has your laptop on their desk and wires into its mainboard, and Coinetic AI Security does not fix CVE-2026-43613. What Coinetic AI Security can do is make sure that a stolen laptop – or a stolen PIN – is not a key to your other computers over the internet: Phone unlock (Device approval): Remote Desktop, or any port you choose, stays invisible to the internet until you unlock it from your registered phone, for a set number of hours, and only for the address your phone is on. Every unlock is signed by your phone's passkey. Someone with your laptop and its saved Remote Desktop connections still finds nothing to connect to – unless they also have your unlocked phone. From your LAN and over a VPN, RDP keeps working. Details: Secure RDP without VPN. Lost phone? Block it: blocking or deleting a phone in Coinetic AI Security closes everything it opened at once. Automatic bans: addresses that guess passwords on RDP, Windows logons, VPN and other services are banned; Under Attack mode closes the admin doors (RDP, SSH, WinRM, SQL Server, SMB / RPC) to the internet in one click while LAN, VPN, web and mail keep running. Ask AI (Pro + AI): right-click a failed login, a ban or a log line and ask, e.g. “Which addresses tried to sign in to this Server by RDP last night, and is anything still open?” – answered from this computer's own Coinetic AI Security data. What it does not cover: the stolen device itself, data already on its disk once BitLocker is unlocked, and cloud services the device signs in to with Windows Hello. For those, the firmware update, a longer PIN and quick revoking are what count. No. The attacker needs the device in their hands and has to open it and attach hardware to the mainboard. Is a 4-digit Windows Hello PIN still safe? On an affected PC that gets stolen, not for long: the paper puts the worst case at about 40 hours. Use at least 8 digits, or letters and digits, especially on laptops. Is there a Microsoft patch? Microsoft did not issue a Windows CVE for it. The fix for the AMD part comes as firmware from AMD through your PC maker (CVE-2026-43613). Microsoft's advice is a longer PIN. Does BitLocker still protect my data? Yes, as long as the startup PIN is long enough and the firmware is updated.
